README Files

README files are a way to document the contents and structure of a folder, helping users locate the information they need. You can use a README to document changes to a repository, and explain how files are named. Please consider adding a README to each repository or including ‘README’ in the name of your overview document.

Registration’s Source Project Is Closed

1 OSF source project is closed. The files metacheck lists below were not read from it — they were retrieved from the OSF registration’s own copy, which is separate from and unaffected by the project’s access setting. Nothing is currently lost, but this is still worth fixing: a closed source project means the files only survive for as long as the registration’s copy does, and anyone who follows the project link itself (rather than the registration) will find it inaccessible.

  • https://osf.io/tw2jv is closed; its files were retrieved from the OSF registration https://osf.io/w9xup/overview, https://osf.io/w9xup.

Consider making the source project openly available.

Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 5 files that software creates by itself, not the authors: operating system (5). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a ._ copy of a .csv for data).

Remove these: Operating system files: macOS adds a __MACOSX folder and a ._ copy of every file it puts in a zip, and .DS_Store files to folders; Windows adds Thumbs.db and desktop.ini. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with zip -r -X, or remove them afterwards with zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store". RStudio session files (.Rproj.user/) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; R history (.Rhistory) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; Jupyter checkpoints (.ipynb_checkpoints/) are automatic copies of notebooks; compiled Python files (__pycache__/, .pyc) are recreated when the code runs; open-document lock files (~$...docx, .~lock...#) are left while a document is open; editor backups (file~, .bak, .swp) and temporary files (.tmp, .temp) are copies a program made by itself.

Keep only on purpose: version control folders (.git, .svn, .hg) hold the project’s history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; editor settings (.idea, .vscode) can hold paths on your own computer. A .gitignore based on GitHub’s templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

To improve (3)

To improve Non-Significant P Value Check

What we found

We found 137 non-significant p values that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

Show details

Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is ‘no effect’, ‘no difference’, or that groups are ‘the same’ after p > 0.05.

It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is ‘not significantly’ different, although this just restates that p > 0.05.

Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values.

Code Comments

Best programming practice is to add comments to code, to explain what the code does (to yourself in the future, or peers who want to re-use your code). All your code files had comments.

Missing Files

All files loaded in the code were present in the repository.

Absolute Paths

Best programming practice is to use relative file paths (e.g., ‘./files’) instead of absolute file paths (e.g., ‘C://Lakens/project_dir/files’) as these folder names do not exist on other computers. No absolute file paths were found in any of the code files.

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No setwd() calls were found in any of the code files.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). No install.packages() calls were found in any of the code files.

Libraries / Imports

Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In all code files, libraries/imports were loaded in one block.

Packages / Dependencies

The code files load 15 distinct packages/libraries: dplyr, forcats, gt, kableExtra, knitr, lavaan, lessSEM, pbmcapply, purrr, see, semTools, stats, tibble, tidyr, tidyverse. These are the names found in the source (no version information is available from static analysis).

Reproducible Environment

No renv.lock file, sessionInfo()/session_info() record, or groundhog/checkpoint date-pin call was found anywhere in the repository. Without one of these, the exact R and package versions used for the analysis are not recoverable, and package versions may drift between when this analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt. Consider depositing an renv.lock (via the renv package), a sessionInfo() text dump, or a groundhog/checkpoint date-pin alongside the code.

Careless Responding

What this does not cover. Only 0 of 14 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

Ethics Approval Check

Power Analysis Check

No power analyses were detected.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

Field Preregistration 1
template_name Secondary Data Preregistration
title Sex moderates the relationship between the Dark Triad and trait aggression
id w9xup
link https://osf.io/w9xup
date_created 2025-10-02T11:18:59.383335
date_modified 2026-10-12T11:44:44.387053
date_registered 2025-10-02T11:18:59.364862
embargo_end_date
ia_url https://archive.org/details/osf-registrations-w9xup-v1
research_questions 1) What is the association between Dark Triad traits and trait aggression?

2) Does sex moderate the association between Dark Triad traits and trait aggression? Prediction 1:

The core of the Dark Triad will be positively associated with all components of aggression (physical, verbal, anger, hostility) in both men and women. Psychopathy will uniquely predict higher levels of physical and verbal aggression, whereas narcissism will uniquely predict lower levels of hostility.

Prediction 2:

Given well-established sex differences in the expression of aggression, we expect men to score higher than women on physical and verbal aggression.

Prediction 3: Considering sex differences in the use of aggression within intrasexual competition, we expect the following sex-specific associations:

a. We predict that the associations that both the core of the Dark Triad and psychopathy have with physical and verbal aggression will be stronger in men than in women, reflecting a greater reliance on direct, contest-based competition among men.

b. We predict that the association between the core of the Dark Triad and hostility will be stronger in women than in men. Additionally, we expect positive associations between Machiavellianism and hostility in women but not in men—consistent with a greater reliance on indirect, scramble competition among women.

In addition to our primary predictions concerning sex as a moderator, we preregister a secondary prediction informed by evolutionary theory on intrasexual competition. Specifically, we will examine whether a short-term mating orientation (STMO) moderates the associations between the Dark Triad and aggression. If intrasexual competition is the driving mechanism between sexual differences, we predict that a higher STMO will strengthen these associations. This prediction is theoretically motivated but considered supplementary to our main specification.
datasets_used The dataset includes a total of 600 Spanish-speaking Chilean participants. The sample comprises university students (n = 316) and members of the general population (n = 284), recruited through public announcements on social networks and the laboratory’s website. Participants were 353 women (M = 26.98 years, SD = 6.56) and 247 men (M = 24.98 years, SD = 5.68). Data collection took place at the Laboratorio de Comportamiento Animal y Humano (LABCAH), Universidad del Desarrollo. The only exclusion criterion was being under 18 years of age.

The data were originally gathered as part of a previous project from one of the coauthors, where measures of trait aggression and Dark Triad traits served as control variables. For the present study, we will analyze these measures as primary outcomes of interest. Participants completed the Buss–Perry Aggression Questionnaire (BPAQ) and the Short Dark Triad questionnaire (SD3), among a broader battery of instruments administered prior to the main experimental procedures. The dataset is cross-sectional, with all measures collected at a single time point.
data_availability The dataset is not publicly available
data_access The finalized dataset has been uploaded to this project as a private file and will be made public at the publishing phase.
access_date The dataset was originally accessed in november 2024, at which time descriptive statistics and a confirmatory factor analysis were conducted. Since that point, the data have not been further analyzed.
data_collection_procedures Data were collected as part of a larger FONDECYT-funded project on aggression and cooperation conducted at the Laboratorio de Comportamiento Animal y Humano (LABCAH), Universidad del Desarrollo. Participants were recruited through public announcements on social networks and the laboratory’s website, as well as university mailing lists. Interested individuals completed an eligibility screening (no couples within the same group), and were scheduled into sessions of six participants each. Group composition was stratified by sex and parental status to create five predefined group types.

Upon arrival, participants completed a battery of self-report questionnaires (including the Short Dark Triad [SD3], the Buss–Perry Aggression Questionnaire [BPAQ], the Multidimensional Sociosexual Orientation Inventory [SOI-M], and the Big Five Inventory [BFI]) before engaging in laboratory behavioral tasks (Point Subtraction Aggression Paradigm, Public Goods Game). Questionnaires were administered in Spanish in a controlled laboratory environment.

The sample is not nationally representative: it consists of university students and volunteers from the general population in central Chile who responded to online and university recruitment efforts. Participants received a payment related to transportation costs (fixed) and another associated with the decisions made in the economic games. Possible biases include self-selection and urban concentration. These factors should be kept in mind when interpreting generalizability.
manipulated_variables Not applicable, this is an observational (correlational) study.
measured_variables Outcome (endogenous) variables (Aggression):

Aggression will be measured with the Spanish adaptation (Valdivia-Peralta et al., 2014) of the Buss–Perry Aggression Questionnaire (Buss & Perry, 1992; BPAQ; 29 items). Items are rated on a 5-point Likert scale (1 = Extremely uncharacteristic of me to 5 = Extremely characteristic of me). The BPAQ produces four subscales, which will be modeled as endogenous latent variables. Following standard practice, covariances across endogenous aggression variables will be freely estimated.

- Physical Aggression (9 items; e.g., “Given enough provocation, I may hit another person”), α = .79.

- Verbal Aggression (5 items; e.g., “My friends say that I’m somewhat argumentative”). α = .69.

- Anger (7 items; e.g., “I have trouble controlling my temper”). α = .77.

- Hostility (8 items; e.g., “I sometimes feel that people are laughing at me behind my back”). α = .75.

Predictor (exogenous) variables (Dark Triad):

Dark Triad traits will be measured with the Spanish adaptation (Pineda et al., 2020) of the Short Dark Triad (Jones & Paulhus, 2014; SD3; 27 items), using 5-point Likert scales (1 = Strongly disagree to 5 = Strongly agree). The SD3 consists of three 9-item subscales:

- Machiavellianism (e.g., “You should wait for the right time to get back at people”), α = .74.

- Narcissism (e.g., “I know that I am special because everyone keeps telling me so”), α = .62.

- Psychopathy (e.g., “People who mess with me always regret it”), α = .63. Due to two psychopathy items with very low standardized loadings (λ < .10), we will conduct sensitivity analyses with and without these items.

- In addition, we will model a Dark Triad Core factor. A bifactor specification will be used: each item loads on a general Dark Core factor as well as its trait-specific factor (Machiavellianism, narcissism, or psychopathy).

Following standard bifactor model practice, we will fix covariances between the Dark Core and the unique trait components to zero. We will test both a specification with zero and free covariances across the unique trait components as a robustness check for the Dark Core as the only source of shared variance among the Dark Triad (Jones & Figueredo, 2013).

Moderator:

- Sex: self-reported as male or female. This variable will be coded as a binary dummy (0 = female, 1 = male).

Control:

- Age: self-reported in years (continuous).

Secondary variables:

- Short Term Mating Orientation (Figueroa et al., 2025; SOI-M, 10 items; e.g., “I can easily imagine myself being comfortable and enjoying casual sex with different partners”). This measure is considered for the secondary prediction, not our main specification.

Residual covariances among items/indicators will be fixed to 0, consistent with standard CFA assumptions. Model fit will be evaluated using common indices available under each estimator (e.g., CFI, TLI, RMSEA, SRMR for ML/WLSMV; posterior predictive checks if Bayesian is needed). We will report all indices provided by the estimation method and evaluate fit holistically, considering conventional guidelines.
missing_data_handling There are no missing data among the variables of interest in this study.
unit_of_analysis Respondents. Considering the data split by sex, 353 participants were women (M = 26.98 years, SD = 6.56) and 247 men (M = 24.98 years, SD = 5.68).
statistical_outliers Outliers will not be excluded; all available data will be included in the preregistered analyses.
sampling_weights No sampling weights.
prior_knowledge Nicolás González: Ran CFA and descriptive statistics at the database consolidation stage. No further knowledge of the data.

José Antonio Muñoz Reyes: Principal Investigator in the project where the data were collected. He has previously used these data as control variables in models predicting other behavioral outcomes. He had no prior knowledge of the specific relationships tested in the present study.

Pablo Polo: Coauthor in the project where the data were collected. He has also previously used these data as control variables in models predicting other behavioral outcomes. He had no prior knowledge of the specific relationships tested in the present study.

Bernhard Fink: No previous knowledge of the data.

Katrin Schäfer: No previous knowledge of the data.

Todd Shackelford: No previous knowledge of the data.

Virgil Zeigler-Hill: No previous knowledge of the data.

Eduardo Galaz: No previous knowledge of the data.
statistical_tests All preregistered analyses will be conducted using structural equation modeling (SEM). The SEM framework is chosen because it allows modeling latent constructs from multiple indicators (Bollen, 1989), and statistically separating the Dark Triad core using a bifactor structure (Rodriguez et al., 2016), as well as testing sex moderation through interaction terms.

Measurement model

* Aggression: Four latent factors from the Buss–Perry Aggression Questionnaire: Physical Aggression (9 items), Verbal Aggression (5 items), Anger (7 items), and Hostility (8 items).

* Dark Triad core: A general latent factor defined by the shared variance across Machiavellianism, Narcissism, and Psychopathy. Loads on every SD3 indicator.

* Unique/residual Dark Triad components: Three latent factors from the Short Dark Triad: Machiavellianism, Narcissism, and Psychopathy (9 items each). Unique variance after accounting for the Dark Triad core.

Structural models

* Model 1 (main effects and sex differences, prediction 1 and 2):
* Physical Aggression ~ Dark Core + residual Psychopathy + Sex
* Verbal Aggression ~ Dark Core + residual Psychopathy + Sex
* Hostility ~ Dark Core + residual Narcissism
* Anger ~ Dark Core

* Model 2 (sex moderation, prediction 3a and 3b): Adds sex × trait interaction terms:
* Physical Aggression ~ Dark Core + residual Psychopathy + Sex + (Sex × Dark Core) + (Sex × residual Psychopathy)
* Verbal Aggression ~ Dark Core + residual Psychopathy + Sex + (Sex × Dark Core) + (Sex × residual Psychopathy)
* Hostility ~ Dark Core + residual Narcissism + residual Machiavellianism + (Sex × Dark Core) + (Sex × residual Machiavellianism)
* Anger ~ Dark Core (no moderation predicted)

In addition to conventional SEM estimates, we will compute trait-level total effects using a Variance-Weighted Latent Effect (VWLE) framework, which reformulates the total effect of a trait as a variance-share–weighted combination of its general (Dark Core) and trait-specific components. In practice, VWLE will be implemented as a non-linear test on model coefficients using the delta method (frequentist) or posterior transformations (Bayesian). The VWLE approach is an ongoing methodological development by the first author; a technical report describing the VWLE framework has been archived in the associated OSF project. The file is private and timestamped to establish priority; full methodological details will be released in a forthcoming publication.

We will add a STMO as a moderator in these models to test our secondary prediction.
inference_criteria Effects will be evaluated with two-tailed tests at α = .05. If Bayesian estimation is needed, we will report 0.95 posterior credibility intervals.
assumption_violation_model_non_convergence Residual psychopathy factor:
Prior work (e.g., de Roos et al., 2017) and our own preliminary CFA with the SD3 indicate that the Dark Core explains nearly all of the variance in psychopathy (λ ≈ .98–.99). This suggests that the unique variance of psychopathy may be negligible once the Dark Core is partialled out. We preregister this as a test of equivalence between SD3 psychopathy and the Dark Core. If the bifactor model fails to converge, or if the residual psychopathy factor is empirically indistinguishable (e.g., all item loadings near zero), we will interpret this as evidence that SD3 psychopathy is fully represented by the Dark Core. In this case, we will remove the residual psychopathy factor from the model and treat psychopathy as equivalent to the Dark Core in subsequent structural analyses.

Distributional assumptions:
If multivariate normality assumptions are violated, models will be estimated using polychoric correlations with robust SEM estimators (e.g., WLSMV) and, where appropriate, ordinal SEM (GSEM).

Generalized non-convergence:
If models fail to converge more broadly, we will re-estimate using Bayesian SEM with weakly informative priors.
reliability_and_robustness_testing Standard errors: All models will be estimated with heteroskedasticity-consistent standard errors.

Bootstrap: We will use bootstrap methods, as appropriate, to refine inference for regression coefficients and global test statistics (e.g., bootstrap-refined t statistics or bootstrap corrections to χ²). Specific bootstrap variants will be selected based on the inferential target and reported transparently.

Cross-validation: We will report within-sample cross-validation (e.g., k-fold) for overall model fit as a descriptive check of replicability.
exploratory_analyses 1) Following Jones & Neria (2015), we will also estimate a model against a general aggression factor (outcome).

2) We will test the full set of Dark Traits (plus core) against each outcome.
paper_id input
