How Ethics Approval Check works

This module searches for statements of ethics approval, IRB approval, institutional review board approval, and related terms.

Patterns are designed to capture:

Human research committee names - Institutional Review Board / IRB (US standard) - Independent Ethics Committee / IEC (ICH-GCP international clinical trial term) - Ethical/Ethics Review Board (generic) - Ethics (Advisory/Review) Committee/Board/Panel/Sub-committee - Research Ethics Committee/Board/Panel (UK/Canada/Australia) - Medical Ethics Committee - Human Subjects/Research Committee / Human Research Ethics (Advisory) Panel - Committee for/on the Protection of Human Subjects - Committee on (Health) Research Ethics - Office of Research Ethics - Abbreviations: IEC, REC, REB, ERB, METC, DEC. REC/REB/ERB/DEC are short enough to collide with unrelated jargon (e.g. REC as a recognition-heuristic model abbreviation, DEC as a decision-task label, Reb as an author surname), so these four require an ethics/approval/committee/board/panel/institutional/ protocol word within ~30 characters in the same sentence. IRB and IEC are kept unconstrained as they are not observed to collide in practice. - Dutch: Medisch-ethische toetsingscommissie (METC) - French: Comité d'éthique / Comité d'Ethique

Animal research committee names - Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee / IACUC (US standard) - Any sentence containing animal(s) and committee (or board/panel) within ~5 words of each other — catches Experimental Animal Care and Use Committee, Animal Ethics Committee, Animal Welfare Board, Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body, etc. - UK: Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body / AWERB - Dutch: Dierexperimentencommissie / DEC (see DEC constraint above); Instantie voor Dierenwelzijn / IvD - German: Tierversuchskommission / TvK (advisory committee under §15 Tierschutzgesetz) - French: Comité d'éthique en expérimentation animale / CEEA; Comité d'éthique animale - Spanish: Comité de ética en experimentación animal / CEEA

Approval phrasing - Ethics/Ethical (approval|clearance) [was] (granted|obtained|received|given|secured) - Ethically approved - Approved by the (ethics|irb|institutional|independent|local|review|research) ... - This/The study/protocol/experiment/procedures/methods/research [was] (approved|reviewed) by - Study was ethically approved - (Followed|met|follow) the ethical (guidelines|standards|requirements) - In accordance with ... ethical (guidelines|standards) - Ethics protocol - Approved under (protocol|reference|number)

Waiver / exemption - Ethics/Ethical (waiver|exemption) - IRB (waiver|exemption|exempt) - Exempted from (ethics|irb|institutional review) - Waived by the (ethics|irb|institutional|review) (committee|board) - Deemed exempt

Declaration of Helsinki - Declaration of Helsinki / Helsinki Declaration

Patterns are NOT designed to capture: - General ethical considerations or ethical dilemmas in study content - Mentions of “ethics” in theoretical or philosophical contexts - Author approval of a manuscript (e.g. “all authors approved the final version”) - Ethical behaviour as a measured variable (e.g. “ethical decision-making”) - URLs containing “ethics” in path components

Live data collection is detected by the internal helper .detect_live_data(), which searches for sentences indicating that data were collected directly from human or animal participants. Papers without any live-data signal are not flagged as missing ethics approval. The helper uses conservative patterns to avoid flagging secondary data analyses, computational experiments, or economics papers that analyse existing survey data. See .detect_live_data() for the full list of patterns and intentional exclusions.

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Power Analysis Check works

This module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. If specified by the user, it also uses a large language model (LLM) to extract information reported in power analyses, including the statistical test, sample size, alpha level, desired level of power, and magnitude and type of effect size.

The Power Analysis Check module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. Without the use of an LLM, the module uses regular expressions to classify the power analysis as a-priori, sensitivity or post-hoc. With the use of an LLM, it checks if the power analysis is reported with all required information.

The regular expressions can miss power analyses, or fail to classify them correctly. The type of power analysis is often difficult to classify, which can easily be solved by explicitly specifying the type of power analysis as ‘a-priori’, ‘sensitivity’, or ‘post-hoc’. Note that ‘post-hoc’ or ‘observed’ power is rarely useful. The LLM can fail to identify information in the paper, and will not have access to information in paragraphs in the paper other than those that contain the word ‘power’. This package was validated by the Metacheck team on articles in Psychological Science.

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine, Daniel Lakens and Cristian Mesquida

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 128 papers with 246 instances of power statements, 203 were correctly detected (true positives), 22 were missed (false negatives) and 21 were incorrectly detected (false positives). Overall, among all instances flagged as power statements, 90.6% were correct (positive predictive value).

How Preregistration Check works

Retrieve information from preregistrations in a standardised way, and make them easier to check.

The Preregistration Check module identifies preregistrations on the OSF and AsPredicted based on links in the manuscript, retrieves the preregistration text, and organizes the information into a template. The module retrieves text from the OSF with its API, and from AsPredicted with ResearchBox’s API when a ResearchBox key is set (see rbox_token()), or else from the preregistration’s web page. The information in the preregistration is returned. An AsPredicted link that could not be read is named in the report, with the reason.

The module can’t extract information from non-structured preregistration templates (i.e., where the preregistration is uploaded in a single text field) and it can’t retrieve information in preregistrations that are stored as text documents on the OSF.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download information from other preregistration sites, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Marginal Significance works

List all sentences that describe an effect as ‘marginally significant’.

The marginal module searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The list of terms is a subset of those listed in a blog post by Matthew Hankins. The module returns all sentences that match terms describing ‘marginally significant’ results.

Some of the terms identified might not be problematic in some contexts, and there are ways to describe ‘marginal significance’ that are not detected by the module.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 51 papers with 87 statements, this module correctly identified 38 statements (true positives) and incorrectly flagged 22 statements (false positives). It failed to detect 27 statements. Thus, among all statements flagged by the module, 63% were genuine cases (positive predictive value). However, the module missed 42% of all true statements (false negative rate).

How StatCheck works

Check consistency of p-values and test statistics

The Statcheck module runs Statcheck. Statcheck searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern, and identifies APA reported statistical tests. More information on the package can be found at https://github.com/cran/statcheck. The module only returns Statcheck results for t-tests and F-tests, as these are the only tests which have been validated, see https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/.

Statcheck was developed by Michèle Nuijten and Sascha Epskamp.

Statcheck considers p = 0.000 an error, as you should report p < 0.001. Furthermore, p < 0.03 is an error if the p-value was 0.031, and one should simply report exact p-values (p = 0.031). Statcheck might miss one-sided tests, and falsely assume the p-value is incorrect. For more information, see StatCheck.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 685 tests with 34 instances of inconsistent reporting, Statcheck correctly detected 34 of them, and incorrectly identified 26. Therefore 0% of true instances were missed, and 43% of detections were false positives. See https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/ for more details of the validation.

How Exact P-Values works

List any p-values reported with insufficient precision (e.g., p < .05 or p = n.s.) or reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000).

This module uses regular expressions to identify p-values. It will flag any values reported as p > ? or p < numbers greater than .001. It will also flag p-values reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000, p = 0.00), which are mathematically impossible — p-values are never exactly zero and should instead be reported as p < .001.

A p-value that is not the result of a test is not flagged: a table note (“* p < .05, ** p < .01”), a figure legend (“Asterisks indicate significant differences (p < .05)”, “Values in bold are significant at p < .05”) or a stated threshold (“p < .05 was considered significant”, “thresholded at p < .001”). GROBID often puts such notes into the running text, so each p-value is judged by the words in its own clause (the text up to a “;” or a full stop), and never left out when a test statistic belongs to it (“F(1, 7) = 8.03, # p < .05”). The column not_a_test of the table says why a p-value was left out (“marker”, “threshold” or “legend”). Notes in other forms, such as a marker after the p-value (“p < .05 (*)“), are still flagged.

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables (as opposed to a table’s footnote text, which the module does see and tries to exclude — see above).

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine and Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 225 papers containing 405 instances of non-exact p-values, the module correctly detected 269 cases (true positives) and incorrectly identified 78 (false positives). It missed 136 instances of imprecisely reported p-values (false negatives) and correctly identified 4557 cases of precisely reported p-values (true negative). Additionally, 78% of positive detections were correct (positive predictive value).

How Non-Significant P Value Check works

This module checks for imprecisely reported p values. If p > .05 is detected, it warns for misinterpretations.

The nonsignificant p-value check searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The module identifies all p-values in a manuscript and selects those that are not reported to be smaller than or equal to 0.05. It returns all sentences containing non-significant p-values.

In the future, the Metacheck team aims to incorporate a machine learning classifier to only return sentences likely to contain misinterpretations. If you want to help to improve the module, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 194 papers with 1602 instances of non-significant p-values, this module correctly detected 1486 of them, and incorrectly identified 153. Additionally, 91% of detections were true instances (positive predictive value). That is, when this module flags non-significant p-values in a paper, it correctly identifies an issue 91% of the time.

How Effect Sizes in t-tests and F-tests works

The Effect Size module checks if effect sizes are correctly reported in t-tests and F-tests.

The Effect Size check searches for regular expressions that match typical ways in which effect sizes are reported. It subsequently checks different ways in which Cohen’s d, g, ηp2, and ωp2 can be computed against the reported value. If effects are missing, or might be incorrect, you the module provides a warning. The module was validated on APA reported statistical tests, and might miss effect sizes that were reported in other reporting styles. It was validated by the Metacheck team on papers published in Psychological Science.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 161 papers with 1469 tests, this module correctly detected 1106 reported effect sizes (true positives) and correctly identified 295 cases where no effect size was present (true negatives). However, it missed 23 that were reported (false negatives), and incorrectly identified 45 effect sizes when none were reported (false positives). Among all instances detected by the module, 96% were true cases (positive predictive value). In a validation against 221 reported Cohen’s d effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 218 cases (99%). In a validation against 485 partial eta-squared effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 480 (99%)

How Codebook Check works

This module checks whether the data columns in a repository are documented in a codebook or README. It locates codebook/readme files, extracts the variable definitions they contain, matches those definitions against the data columns extracted by data_check, and reports documentation coverage: how many data columns are documented, and which documented variables are never used.

The Codebook Check module consumes the columns and file classification produced by data_check (and, transitively, repo_check). Files classified as codebook or readme are parsed with parse_codebook(), which reads structured tables (CSV/TSV/Excel with a variable-name column and a label column), embedded labels in haven files (SPSS/Stata/SAS), and plain text from rich-text formats (docx/pdf/rtf/odt). Embedded haven labels from data files are also harvested directly.

Each data column is then matched against the parsed variable definitions with match_column_labels(), using normalised-name matching with experiment-group scoping, haven-label priority, and rule-based label-equivalence merging.

Beyond the variable label, the module harvests the DDI-style per-variable properties a source supplies: the value labels / code list (the 1=“Strongly disagree”…5=“Strongly agree” mapping — from SPSS/Stata value labels and from a codebook “values”/“coding” column), the missing-value scheme (which codes denote missingness, from haven declared missings and labels that read as “refused”/“n/a”), and question text and columns when present. These are carried onto the matched data columns and exported into the Psych-DS variableMeasured (as a schema.org code list plus namespaced metacheck: fields).

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE). When llm_use(TRUE), three optional LLM tiers run: parsing unstructured codebook text that the rules could not handle, fuzzy-matching still-unlabelled columns to still-unmatched codebook variables, and merging conflicting label definitions into a single canonical label.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the codebook_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Repository Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories.

The Repository Check module lists files on the OSF, GitHub, ResearchBox, DSpace (PsychArchives and other legacy- and DSpace 7-based installations), Zenodo, Dataverse, Figshare, Dryad, ReShare, 4TU.ResearchData, Mendeley Data, DataONE (Arctic Data Center, KNB, and other member nodes), and LDbase based on links in the manuscript.

Listing a repository’s files never requires an API key, but some hosts answer faster or more completely with one: OSF allows 100 requests/hour unauthenticated versus 10,000/day with a token (see [osf_pat()]), and Dryad enforces a strict per-IP daily quota on repeated listing (see cache below). Dryad is a special case beyond rate limits: listing a Dryad dataset’s files works without a key, but actually downloading file CONTENTS from Dryad fails with HTTP 401 unless a key is set, even for a fully public dataset (see [dryad_pat()] or [dryad_auth()]). Since this module only lists files and never downloads their contents itself, that limitation applies to data_check and code_check (which do download content), not here – see their own documentation.

When a linked OSF page is a registration, its registered_from project (the one it was registered from, which the manuscript itself may never link directly) is also checked: if that project is public its files are listed under its own URL, and if it is closed or otherwise inaccessible the report flags it explicitly, since some registrations only describe their content rather than mirroring it.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download files from additional data repositories reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the repo_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Code Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories checked by repo_check about code files (R, Python, SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, MATLAB).

The Code Check module checks R (also R Markdown and Quarto), Python (also Jupyter notebooks), SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, and MATLAB files, using regular expressions to check the code; JASP files are listed but not read. The language of a Quarto document or a notebook is read from the file itself (its engine or kernel), not from its extension. The regular expression search will detect the number of comments, the lines at which libraries/imports are loaded, attempts to detect absolute paths to files, setwd() and install.packages() calls, and lists files that are loaded, and checks if these files are in the repository; R code is also parsed. The module will return suggestions to improve the code if there are no comments, if libraries/imports are loaded in lines further than 4 lines apart, if files that are loaded are not in the repository, if absolute file paths, setwd() or install.packages() are found, and if R code cannot be parsed.

The regular expressions can miss information in code files, or falsely detect parts of the code as a fixed file path. Libraries/imports might be loaded in one block, even if there are more than 3 intermittent lines. The module was tried out internally on papers published in Psychological Science, but has not been formally validated. There might be valid reasons why some loaded files can’t be shared, but the module can’t evaluate these reasons, and always gives a warning.

The module also checks whether the repository pins the R/package versions the analysis actually depended on: an renv.lock file (parsed for the R version and every locked package + its version/source), a sessionInfo()/sessioninfo::session_info() text dump (matched by filename — sessionInfo.txt/session_info.txt and similar, or embedded in a README), or a groundhog::groundhog.library()/checkpoint::checkpoint() date-pin call in the code (a bare library(groundhog)/library(checkpoint) does not count — the pinning call itself must be present). When none of these is found, the report flags it as a reproducibility gap: package versions may drift between when the analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt.

If you want to extend the package to perform additional checks on code files, or make the checks work on other types of code files, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

Checking code requires downloading its file contents. For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this never succeeds unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (listing the repository’s files does not need one). Without a key, every Dryad-hosted code file is listed but unchecked, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures recorded in the manifest.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Raphael Merz

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the code_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Data Check works

This module classifies the files in a repository into semantic types (data, codebook, code, software, output, supplemental, readme, asset, other) and, for tabular data files, extracts each column’s type and summary statistics.

The Data Check module consumes the file list produced by repo_check (or any files added via local_path). Each file is classified with rule-based heuristics layered over metacheck’s file_category() and file_types: file names matching README / codebook patterns win first, then an extension crosswalk, then format-locked extension overrides. For every file classified as tabular data that is available locally, the module reads the file head, describes each column with data_col_facets() and computes summary statistics for numeric columns. Every sheet of a spreadsheet that holds a table is read: a file with several such sheets has its columns under source_file = "file.xlsx [sheet]", and the sheet column names the sheet of any spreadsheet with several sheets; a sheet of notes or a codebook is treated as documentation when the file has another table. Following DDI, a column is described by orthogonal facets rather than a single type: representation (numeric/text/datetime/code — how it is stored), measurement_level (Stevens: nominal/ordinal/interval/ratio), concept (what it measures: reaction_time/age/gender/likert/id/…), role (identifier/measure/condition/timestamp), unit, and a quality state (ok/empty/constant). Concepts are detected by name+value rules (the demographic concepts via data_check_demographic()); when llm_use(TRUE) the model fills concepts and measurement levels the rules left blank. Qualtrics survey exports are recognised (data_check_is_qualtrics()): their extra header rows are stripped so columns type correctly, and the reserved response-metadata columns (StartDate, Duration, Finished, …) are tagged.

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE): columns the rules cannot resolve (ambiguous 3–20-unique integers, ambiguous character columns) fall back to continuous / text respectively. When llm_use(TRUE), ambiguous columns and unresolved file types (other) are sent to llm() for optional refinement, and every file is assigned a study group (ex1, pilot2, shared, …) so that multi-study repositories can be recognised (used by psychds_check). Without an LLM the study group is left NA (unknown).

Column extraction requires files to be readable from disk. Files fetched by repo_check from OSF/GitHub/etc. without a local copy (file_location is NA) are classified but not column-extracted; pass local_path to point at a downloaded copy of the repository.

For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this means column extraction never happens unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (dataset listing and metadata do not need one). Without a key, every Dryad file stays classified but un-downloaded, column_n is 0, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures. A one-time session message is also shown (see repo_check) the first time a Dryad dataset is encountered with no key set.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the data_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Reproducibility Check works

This module assesses whether a paper’s R and Python code can be run on its data. It works in two phases. The static phase (always run) collects the package dependencies the code declares, rewrites the data-file paths that do not work in the repository as the authors organised it, works out the order the scripts must run in, and diagnoses why any referenced input file is unavailable — reporting what a reproduction attempt would involve and where it is likely to break. The execution phase (opt-in, execute = TRUE) then actually runs the code: it copies the repository into a throwaway directory, optionally installs the declared dependencies into a throwaway library, runs each script in order in an isolated subprocess with a per-script timeout, and captures the outcome and full output of each run.

By default (execute = FALSE) the module does not run any code — it performs only static analysis: reading dependencies with the same extractors as code_check, finding the files the code references in the repository, and building a run-order dependency graph. It reports what would be installed and run rather than doing it.

When execute = TRUE, the module additionally runs the downloaded code on your machine — a deliberate, opt-in action gated behind that argument (callr is required for R code). Each script runs in an isolated subprocess so a crash cannot take down the R session; note this isolates crashes, not the filesystem or network. Installs (when install_missing = TRUE) and the throwaway run library never touch your main R library. Each script’s outcome is one of ran_ok, errored, timed_out, dependency_unavailable, not_parsed, run_by_source (an R script another script runs with source(), which is run only inside that script, since on its own it lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first), run_by_import (a Python file other files import, a module rather than a script, unless it has an if __name__ == "__main__": block), jags_model (a JAGS or BUGS model saved with an R extension, which another script reads) or not_r_content (a file that is not R at all, such as a JSON or HTML dump); these last two are not run and are not failures. python2 marks Python 2 code that was not run. With sandbox = "docker" such code runs with Python 2.7 (option metacheck.docker_image_py2; FALSE turns this off), which modifications records; it is never converted, since that can change results. defines_functions is a file that only defines functions, which is used, not run (table$used_by names the scripts that use it), and not_analysis is a file of software rather than of the analysis: a package’s code, tests, documentation or setup.py, a copy of a tool, a web application, a script a program wrote (table$not_analysis_why says which); neither is run or counted as a script. docker_failed means the container never started, which says nothing about the script, so it keeps the light from being green but does not make it red. needs_a_person is a script that stopped because it asks a person to choose a file or answer a question, or that starts an app, and needs_internet one that stopped because the network is off in a Docker run, or, with internet = TRUE, could not reach what it asked for; download_too_large is a script stopped for downloading more than the limits allow (see internet), and out_of_memory one that, or a program it started (such as a compiler), ran out of the memory each script may use. All four are treated the same way. not_downloaded is a script that stopped on a file the repository lists but that was not downloaded, such as one over max_file_size: it could not be tried, so it is not counted as a script that did not reproduce (summary_table$repro_not_downloaded_n counts them apart). A timeout means “still running at the cutoff”, not a failure, so raise timeout for legitimately long-running (e.g. Bayesian) scripts. dependency_unavailable means the script’s own package could not be installed from live CRAN, the CRAN Archive, or a named GitHub/URL source — an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper’s code, so unlike errored/timed_out it does not force the traffic light red. The full stdout/stderr of every run is kept in the result’s run_results (the report shows it in per-script dropdowns, capped for readability). The traffic light reflects the STATIC readiness signals by default, but an execution error (errored/timed_out) does recolour it to red — a script that crashes on its own analysis is a genuine reproduction failure. A script that fails with could not find function is run once more with the library() calls the project’s other scripts make added at its top (or the one package that exports the function, or magrittr for %>%), and a script that then runs is reported as reproducible only after that repair.

Dependencies are reported name-only, with the source (CRAN, GitHub, or a base package already shipped with R) — static analysis of the code cannot know which version was used, and running against current package versions is itself informative: a break argues the authors should have pinned versions. When the repository does record versions, a run with recorded_versions = TRUE installs the packages the scripts load at those versions, but it does not change the R version, which remains a limitation of the check.

Run order is derived from read-after-write data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads must run first), source() edges, and numeric filename prefixes as a weak tie-breaker. Ambiguous orderings, dependency cycles, and inputs a script reads but that no earlier script produces (and that are not in the repository) are surfaced as warnings, since these are the situations most likely to make an otherwise-correct reproduction fail.

Python code (.py files, and notebooks and Quarto documents whose code is Python, from which the code is extracted first) goes through the same two phases, reported in its own “Python code” section. Each file is checked for syntax errors with Python’s own parser when a Python interpreter (python, or else python3) is available; dependencies are read from the import statements, with versions from a requirements.txt or pyproject.toml when there is one, and installed with pip; each script runs as its own python process (processx is required), so unlike R scripts, a name one script defines is not available to another. When no Python interpreter is available, the Python files are reported as not run and the R results are still returned. Statistics the Python scripts print are compared with the paper together with the R output and any self-reproducible output (JASP/jamovi, SPSS-Viewer, notebook outputs).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the ref_doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited (currently, a warning is provided regardless of whether the replication/reproduction study is already cited).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the ref_doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Full text

Abstract

Although the Dark Triad (i.e., psychopathy, Machiavellianism, and narcissism) has been consistently linked to aggressive behaviors such as bullying and violence, two important questions about these associations remain unresolved. First, little is known about how they differ between women and men. Second, it remains unclear how factor overlap affects their substantive interpretation. Drawing on evolutionary accounts of intrasexual competition, we predict stronger associations with physical and verbal aggression in men and hostility in women. We test these predictions on Short Dark Triad and Buss and Perry Aggression Questionnaire data from 600 Chilean adults, using bifactor (S-1) structural equation modeling. We find that Machiavellianism predicts all aggression outcomes, psychopathy-specific variance positively predicts physical aggression, and narcissism-specific variance negatively predicts hostility. Sex differences in aggression overlap with sex differences in aversive traits, but none of the Dark Triad-aggression associations consistently differ by sex. By introducing the variance-weighted latent effect (VWLE), we provide the first substantive translation of these bifactor associations. VWLE clarifies how reference facet and trait-specific associations reinforce one another for psychopathy but largely cancel out for narcissism, making the implications of residual coefficients explicit.

1. Introduction

A defining feature of individuals high in Dark Triad traits (i.e., psychopathy, Machiavellianism, and narcissism) is their heightened propensity for aggressive behavior (Furnham et al., 2013). These traits have been linked to various forms of aggression, including bullying (Baughman et al., 2012; van Geel et al., 2017), support for politically motivated violence (Nai & Young, 2024), and criminal behavior (Brugués & Caparrós, 2022; Hampejs et al., 2025). However, these investigations have rarely considered sex differences. A substantial body of evidence suggests that men and women differ in the expression of aggression (Archer, 2004), with these differences often attributed to evolutionary pressures such as sexual selection (Archer, 2009). This raises the possibility that men and women high in aversive personality traits may express distinct aggressive strategies in pursuit of their goals, but the literature has yet to elucidate this relationship. Moreover, previous research has not yet resolved how overlap among Dark Triad traits affects the substantive interpretation of their relationships with aggression. We examine whether sex moderates the relationship between Dark Triad traits and dispositional aggression, and introduce the variance-weighted latent effect (VWLE) to clarify the interpretation of these associations in the presence of factor overlap.

1.1. Intrasexual competition

Sexual selection theory explains the evolution of traits that enhance mating success through two primary mechanisms: intersexual selection and intrasexual competition, whereby individuals compete with same-sex rivals for access to potential mates (D. M. Buss, 1989; D. M. Buss & Schmitt, 2019; Darwin, 1871; Puts, 2016). In humans, females are argued to have faced evolutionary pressures associated with greater fitness costs from physical aggression (Campbell, 1999). These pressures thus tend to disfavor direct confrontation with same-sex rivals (Archer, 2009; Campbell, 2006) and instead promote reliance on indirect competitive tactics such as derogation of competitors, social exclusion, and alliance formation-as forms of intrasexual competition (Björkqvist, 2018; Vaillancourt, 2013). This approach is often characterized as scramble competition (Benenson & Abadzi, 2020). In contrast, males tend to exhibit greater variability in reproductive success (Brown et al., 2009), which fosters strategies that emphasize direct, often aggressive, competition for mates, including dominance displays and physical confrontations (Archer, 2009; Campbell, 2006). This pattern has been referred to as contest competition (Puts et al., 2015). Therefore, sex differences are expected to shape both the prevalence and form of aggressive behavior.

1.2. Aggression

Aggression is a multifaceted construct encompassing instrumental, affective, and cognitive components. The instrumental component 1 involves the intentional delivery of harm to others and can be expressed in both verbal and physical forms. The affective component centers on the emotional experience of anger that prepares the individual for aggressive action. The cognitive component, often referred to as hostility, includes negative thoughts and beliefs that motivate aggressive behavior (A. H. Buss & Perry, 1992). Aggression can be expressed through both direct and indirect forms. Direct aggression entails overt acts such as physical violence or verbal attacks, whereas indirect aggression involves covert strategies, such as manipulating others to harm the target (Björkqvist et al., 1992).

From an evolutionary perspective, aggression is broadly defined as behavior aimed at inflicting costs on others, with its role in intrasexual competition among its most salient functions (D. M. Buss & Shackelford, 1997). Consistent with this evolutionary function, research has established sex differences in preferred forms of aggression. Men display more direct and riskier forms of aggressive behavior, a finding that is well-documented across studies (Daly & Wilson, 1990 , 2001). For example, global crime data from 2021 indicate that 81% of homicide victims and 90% of individuals investigated for murder were male (United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime, 2023). In contrast, women and girls are more likely to engage in indirect forms of aggression (Björkqvist, 2018; Björkqvist et al., 1992).

At the component level, men score higher than women on trait measures of aggression, particularly in the physical dimension (Jain et al., 2023). Men also exhibit higher levels of verbal aggression than women, although the magnitude of this difference is smaller than that observed for physical aggression (Archer, 2004; Björkqvist et al., 1992). In contrast, research has found no reliable sex differences in experienced anger or hostility (Archer, 2004; A. H. Buss & Perry, 1992; Jain et al., 2023; Muñoz-Reyes et al., 2018; Romero et al., 2024; Santisteban et al., 2007; Webster et al., 2014). However, among the components of aggression, hostility has shown the strongest association with intrasexual forms of indirect aggression (Archer & Webb, 2006). This suggests that hostility may reflect not only antagonistic cognition, but also may play a role in the planning and execution of indirect aggressive strategies. As such, hostility may serve as a useful proxy for identifying individuals predisposed to indirect aggression.

1.3. The Dark Triad

Beyond sex differences, aversive personality traits have attracted attention as contributors to individual differences in aggression (Jain et al., 2023; D. N. Jones & Neria, 2015; S. E. Jones et al., 2011; Paulhus et al., 2018). The classic Dark Triad-consisting of psychopathy (lack of self-control and impulsivity), Machiavellianism (strategic-calculating orientation), and narcissism (grandiose identity)-was originally conceptualized based on the callous and manipulative tendencies shared by the three constituent traits (Paulhus & Williams, 2002). These shared tendencies have often been attributed to an underlying Dark Core factor, with some accounts arguing that individual traits reflect particular deviations from this general factor (Bader et al., 2023). Several studies suggest that the Dark Core is effectively defined by a callousness and manipulation factor, which accounts for most of the shared variance among Dark Triad traits (D. N. Jones & Figueredo, 2013; Vize et al., 2020). Whether it is distinguishable from antagonism-i.e., low agreeableness-remains a debated topic (Horsten et al., 2024; Rose et al., 2023).

From an evolutionary perspective, aversive personality traits have been explained through the mechanisms of frequency-dependent selection, where a balance of genotypes may favor the continuous presence of exploitative individuals (Book & Quinsey, 2004; Wilson, 1994; Wilson et al., 1996), and phenotypic plasticity, where life history theory accounts for fast vital trajectories (Book et al., 2015; Davis et al., 2019; Hawley, 2006; McDonald et al., 2012). However, prior work has rarely considered sex differences in the expression or function of aversive traits. Existing evidence indicates that men score higher than women across the Dark Triad, with especially pronounced differences in psychopathy (Bucher et al., 2023; Muris et al., 2017). Aversive traits may be particularly relevant to intrasexual competition, where attributes such as callousness could facilitate dominance over same-sex rivals or strategic rival derogation. Given that men are more likely to engage in intense and risky forms of intrasexual competition (Puts et al., 2015), aversive traits may confer competitive advantages that have greater utility for males, helping to explain their higher prevalence in men (Jonason & Webster, 2010).

Research employing multidimensional measures of dispositional aggression has found positive associations with the Dark Triad (Jain et al., 2023; D. N. Jones & Neria, 2015; Zaitsu, 2024). For example, D. N. Jones and Neria (2015) reported that the Dark Core is associated with a general aggression factor. However, when examining zero-order correlations, one nonsignificant relationship emerged between narcissism and hostility-a finding replicated in other studies (e.g., Jain et al., 2023). This pattern suggests that narcissism contains a unique suppressor component that may reduce its overall association with hostility, even though the Dark Core is positively related to it (D. N. Jones & Neria, 2015; Zaitsu, 2024). In contrast, the unique component of psychopathy consistently predicts physical aggression (Jain et al., 2023; D. N. Jones & Neria, 2015; Zaitsu, 2024) and may extend to verbal aggression (Jain et al., 2023) and anger (Jain et al., 2023; Zaitsu, 2024).

1.4. Predictions

(1) Based on prior findings, we predict that the shared variance of the Dark Triad (i.e., Dark Core) will be positively associated with all components of aggression in both men and women. In addition, psychopathy is expected to exhibit unique positive associations with physical and verbal aggression, whereas narcissism is anticipated to show a unique negative association with hostility. (2) Given well-established sex differences in the expression of aggression, we expect men to score higher than women on physical and verbal aggression. (3) Considering sex differences in the use of aggression within intrasexual competition, we expect the following sex-specific associations: (a) The associations of both the shared variance and psychopathy with physical and verbal aggression will be stronger in men than in women, reflecting a greater reliance on direct, contest-based competition among men. (b) The association between the shared variance and hostility will be stronger in women than in men.

Additionally, Machiavellianism will be positively associated with hostility in women but not in men, consistent with a greater reliance on indirect, scramble competition among women.

1.5. Factor overlap: The case of the Dark Triad

Evaluating the associations of the Dark Triad with external outcomes such as aggression leads to an open methodological challenge: high intercorrelations between traits make it difficult to disentangle their unique contributions. This challenge has generated debate over appropriate statistical approaches and theoretical interpretations (Furnham et al., 2014; Sleep et al., 2017). One widely adopted solution has been to isolate the shared variance using bifactor models (McLarnon & Tarraf, 2017) and analyze it separately from the unique components of each trait. However, this approach introduces a secondary challenge. Namely, bifactor models explicitly residualize traits relative to one another, raising concerns about whether their results can be interpreted as associations involving the original constructs (Hoyle et al., 2023; Miller et al., 2019). In particular, effects of residual components may not hold at the first-order level due to suppressionfoot_2 , and may imply associations that are hard to justify substantively (Sleep et al., 2017).

The direct structural interpretation of bifactor residual coefficients is semi-partial (Eid et al., 2018). For example, in an S -1 model with Machiavellianism as the reference facet, the psychopathy coefficient indicates how aggression varies with psychopathy above or below the level expected from a person's Machiavellianism (Eid et al., 2017). Yet conditioning at the measurement stage leaves the magnitudes of those expectations and departures, and thus the structure against which coefficients are interpreted, implicit. To narrow this gap, we present a pilot implementation of the VWLE, a technique that consolidates this information for substantive interpretation. VWLE is the estimand that specifically targets conceptual overlap by weighting shared and residual component contributions to reconstruct a trait's first-order association with an outcome.

1.6. Present study

In this study, we (1) examine whether the relationships between the Dark Triad and aggression differ between women and men, and (2) use the VWLE to illustrate how factor overlap can affect the substantive conclusions drawn for these relationships.

2. Materials and methods

>Materials and methods

2.1. Participants

The study includes a total of 600 Chilean participants, all of whom are Spanish-speaking. The sample is composed of university students (n = 316) and members of the general population (n = 284), recruited through public announcements on social networks and the laboratory's website. The sample consists of 353 women (M = 26.98, SD = 6.56, range = 18-47 years) and 247 men (M = 24.98, SD = 5.68, range = 18-44 years). The data were collected at the Laboratorio de Comportamiento Animal y Humano (LABCAH), Universidad del Desarrollo. No exclusion criteria were specified aside from being at least 18 years of age.

2.2. Measurements

>Measurements

BPAQ.

Dispositional aggression is measured with a Spanish-validated (Valdivia-Peralta et al., 2014) version of the Buss and Perry Aggression Questionnaire (BPAQ -A. H. Buss & Perry, 1992). This questionnaire is a widely used self-report measure evaluating individual differences in aggression across four dimensions: Physical Aggression (e.g., "Given enough provocation, I may hit another person"), Verbal Aggression (e.g., "My friends say that I'm somewhat argumentative"), Hostility ("I sometimes feel that people are laughing at me behind my back"), and Anger (e.g., "I have trouble controlling my temper"). The BPAQ comprises 29 items rated on a 5-point Likert scale ranging from 1 ("Extremely uncharacteristic of me") to 5 ("Extremely characteristic of me") (A. H. Buss & Perry, 1992).

SD3.

Dark Triad personality traits are measured with a Spanish-validated (Pineda et al., 2020) version of the Short Dark Triad questionnaire (SD3 -D. N. Jones & Paulhus, 2014), which assesses Machiavellianism (e.g., "You should wait for the right time to get back at people"), psychopathy (e.g., "People who mess with me always regret it") and narcissism (e.g., "I know that I am special because everyone keeps telling me so"). The SD3 consists of 27 items, with nine items dedicated to each subscale. Participants respond to each item on a 5-point Likert scale ranging from 1 ("Strongly disagree") to 5 ("Strongly agree") (D. N. Jones & Paulhus, 2014).

We obtain reliability estimates broadly consistent with prior findings across scales (see Table A3). Self-reported sex is coded as a binary dummy (0 = female,1 = male), and age in years is used as a control variable and is standardized prior to analysis.

2.3. Procedure

The data for this study were collected as part of a previous project in which measures of aggression and Dark Triad traits served as control variables (Muñoz-Reyes et al., 2023). Participants responded to the BPAQ and the SD3 questionnaires among a battery of tests before the main experimental procedures.

Note.

Entries are zero-order correlations estimated from correlated-factor measurement models of the study variables. Column numbers correspond to the numbered variables in the rows.

2.4. Analyses

We use structural equation modeling (SEM) to evaluate our predictions. We start by testing for measurement invariance between sexes in each questionnaire to assess whether the constructs are measured comparably in women and men. We then use lasso regularized multigroup (Huang, 2018) confirmatory factor analyses (CFA) to identify non-invariant items for our primary partial-scalar-invariant measurement specifications (Putnick & Bornstein, 2016). Because the Dark Triad traits are entered as simultaneous predictors, we specify a bifactor S -1 measurement model (Eid et al., 2017), with Machiavellianism defining the reference facet (Postigo et al., 2024). Therefore, psychopathy and narcissism represent specific components residualized relative to the reference Machiavellianism. Aggression dimensions are measured under a standard correlated four-factor model.

To directly parameterize the relevant sex differences, including interaction terms, we use a two-stage plausible-value (PV) multiple-imputation (MI) approach (Rubin, 1987). In the first stage, we estimate separate multigroup CFA measurement models for each questionnaire to fix the meaning of constructs, and then combine them into a composed (Bee et al., 2023) imputation model with covariates. Only cross-questionnaire covariances and covariances with covariates are freely estimated in the imputation model. This sex-stratified imputation model (von Hippel, 2009) then satisfies the congeniality requirement of PV inference by including all variables entering the second stage (Asparouhov & Muthén, 2010). In the second stage, we fit the structural models to multiple draws from this imputation model and pool the results, propagating latent measurement uncertainty into the structural estimates.

All predictions involving the shared variance of the scale (i.e., Dark Core) are indirectly assessed by the inclusion of the reference facet carrying it. Under the bifactor S-1 measurement model, this shared variance is not separately identifiable from the chosen reference facet (Eid et al., 2017). The first confirmatory model evaluates Prediction 1-that the reference facet will be positively associated with all aggression components, psychopathy with physical and verbal aggression, and narcissism negatively with hostility. The second model adds the confirmatory interactions for Prediction 3a-that the associations of the reference facet and psychopathy with physical and verbal aggression will be stronger among men-and Prediction 3b-that the associations of the reference facet with hostility will be stronger among women. Moderation involving a separate Machiavellianism-specific component cannot be assessed in this parameterization. All confirmatory models control for age and freely estimate residual covariances among the aggression outcomes. Prediction 2-that men will report greater physical and verbal aggression-is evaluated using unconditional sex differences. Subsequent exploratory models include all interactions between the Dark Triad components and sex to situate the focal effects within the broader pattern of associations.

Measurement and structural models are estimated using robust maximum likelihood. Full-sample analyses use 500 MI draws, with asymptotic inference based on pooling within-and between-imputation variance according to Rubin's (1987) total variance rule. Standardized coefficients and coefficients of determination are obtained by standardizing, then pooling (van Ginkel, 2020). As a robustness check, we perform a fullpipelinefoot_3 percentile-t bootstrap (Hall, 1986) with 9, 999 resamples, using 25 MI draws per resample. All tests are two-tailed with α = 0.05.

We further present the pilot implementation of the VWLE-an ongoing methodological development by the first author-which translates partial effects from the reducedform bifactor model to the first-order construct level for substantive interpretation (see Appendix E for derivation and implementation details). For non-reference traits, the implemented oblique-least-squares VWLE releases conditioning on the reference facet while retaining adjustment for sibling-specific components and covariates. VWLE estimates are presented descriptively and are not used for confirmatory inference.

All analyses are conducted in R version 4.5.3 using the packages lavaan version 0.6-21 (Rosseel, 2012) for SEM; semTools version 0.5-8 (Jorgensen et al., 2026) for PVs; and lessSEM version 1.5.7 (Orzek, 2023; Orzek et al., 2023) for regularized CFA.

3. Results

Main diagnostics broadly support metric invariance between sexes across scales, whereas evidence is only mixed for full scalar invariance under conventional guidelines (see Section A.3). Figure 1 presents standardized scores by sex, with significance indicators based on differences between these means. Naïve sum scores indicate that men score higher than women across physical aggression, verbal aggression, Machiavellianism, psychopathy, and narcissism, whereas women score higher in anger, and hostility does not differ by sex.

Under partial scalar-invariant specifications, men retain substantially higher scores across physical aggression (β = 0.614, p < .001, η² semi = .092), Machiavellianism (β = 0.604, p < .001, η² semi = .089), psychopathy (β = 0.473, p < .001, η² semi = .055) and narcissism (β = 0.461, p < .001, η² semi = .052). Women retain a higher score in anger (β = -0.441, p < .001, η² semi = .047), whereas the raw difference in verbal aggression dissipates (β = 0.061, p = .475, η² semi = .001). Hostility remains broadly equivalent between sexes (β = 0.042, p = .641, η² semi = .001). Table 2 presents the confirmatory structural models. C1 includes the Dark Triad main effects specified in Prediction 1; C2 adds the confirmatory interactions specified in Predictions 3a and 3b. The reference coefficient expresses the first-order association for Machiavellianism, while psychopathy and narcissism coefficients in the structural block describe residual associations. The VWLE block translates the latter into first-order associations. With respect to the Dark Triad, the reference Machiavellianism positively predicts physical aggression (β = 0.458, p < .001, η² semi = .217), verbal aggression (β = 0.384, p < .001, η² semi = .135), hostility (β = 0.558, p < .001, η² semi = .286), and anger (β = 0.377, p < .001, η² semi = .130) in C1 (see Table D1 for anger estimates). The psychopathy component positively predicts physical aggression (β = 0.284, p < .001, η² semi = .090), whereas the narcissism component negatively predicts hostility (β = -0.209, p < .001, η² semi = .044). Controlling for the Dark Triad, women's scores increase relative to men across outcomes. Sex differences shrink in physical aggression (β = 0.300, p < .001, η² semi = .023), increase in anger (β = -0.639, p < .001, η² semi = .091), and appear in hostility (β = -0.232, p = .003, η² semi = .012) once aversive traits are accounted for. All associations in C1 are preserved under percentile-t bootstrap inference. Including the interaction terms in C2 reveals only a small difference in the association of psychopathy with physical aggression in men (β = -0.179, p = .005, η² semi = .009). The negative sign indicates a weaker, but still positive, association among men. However, this difference is not supported under percentile-t bootstrap inference (p = .176). The associations of the reference Machiavellianism do not differ between women and men across physical aggression (β = -0.039, p = .558, η² semi = .001), verbal aggression (β = 0.010, p = .873, η² semi < .001) and hostility (β = -0.087, p = .180, η² semi = .002). VWLE estimates translate these component-level coefficients into the original Dark Triad coordinates. The reference Machiavellianism and specific-component associations reinforce one another when their directions align, but cancel one another when their signs oppose. Narcissism provides the clearest example: its negative specific association with hostility is largely offset by its positive reference contribution, yielding a negligible first-order association.

Machiavellianism

Table 3 presents an exploratory model including all Dark Triad main terms across aggression equations. It reveals that psychopathy parallels the broad pattern observed for the reference Machiavellianism, with moderate to large associations with hostility (η² semi = .071) and verbal aggression (η² semi = .152), and very large associations with physical aggression (η² semi = .248) and anger (η² semi = .242). In the jointly estimated system, excluding psychopathy from an equation leaves psychopathy-related variation in its residual, which may attenuate its estimated associations elsewhere through the correlated residuals. This is especially relevant to the verbal aggression estimate, which changes dramatically relative to the confirmatory specification. Expanding the conditioning set also enhances the scores of women relative to men even further, with meaningful changes to verbal aggression (η² semi = .014) and anger estimates (η² semi = .125). Including all Dark Triad interactions with sex likewise provides no support for the predicted sex differences (see Table D2).

Finally, Figure 2 displays the first-order associations implied by the VWLE estimates from the exploratory model. Descriptively, psychopathy generally shows the strongest associations across aggression outcomes, followed by Machiavellianism, which matches it in hostility. Even accounting for its shared-variance component, the associations of narcissism with trait aggression are very small.

4. Discussion

We examine how Dark Triad traits relate to different forms of dispositional aggression in women and men. Our analyses reveal broad support for Prediction 1: the reference facet of the Dark Triad is positively associated with all aggression outcomes, psychopathy has a unique positive association with physical aggression, and narcissism has a unique negative association with hostility. Psychopathy also shows the expected unique association with verbal aggression, but only once its associations across all correlated aggression outcomes are appropriately represented. Prediction 2 receives partial support: we find sex differences in raw aggression scores for physical and verbal aggression in favor of men, but only the difference in physical aggression remains supported after accounting for measurement non-invariance. Finally, Prediction 3 receives no support: we do not find larger associations with the Dark Triad in physical and verbal aggression for men, nor in hostility for women. Sex differences involving a Machiavellianism-specific component are not evaluated.

In light of Machiavellianism's small facet-specific variance in the higher-order representation (see Table A6), its associations with aggression outcomes support the view that the antagonistic features shared across Dark Triad traits (Paulhus & Williams, 2002) represent a general disposition toward aggression (D. N. Jones & Neria, 2015). Psychopathy nevertheless contributes beyond the reference facet. These unique associations may be explained by psychopathy's impulsive tendencies (Paulhus & Williams, 2002), which seem not only to facilitate the behavioral expression of aggression (Bresin, 2019) but also enhance its cognitive and affective components. The particularly strong association of psychopathy with anger deserves special attention. As Archer and Webb (2006) note, BPAQ anger items overlap with direct measures of impulsiveness, suggesting that part of the association of psychopathy with anger may reflect common item content rather than an underlying structural relationship.

The negative unique association between narcissism and hostility points to a different decomposition: once the shared callousness and manipulation variance represented by the reference Machiavellianism is removed, the remaining narcissism component may more strongly reflect its concern for social status (Zeigler-Hill et al., 2019 , 2021). This is consistent with the SD3 measurement of narcissism primarily reflecting the trait's agentic-extraverted facet (Crowe et al., 2019). Moreover, although narcissistic individuals respond aggressively when ego-threatened (Krizan & Johar, 2015; Stucke & Sporer, 2002), these context-dependent reactions may not be fully captured by trait-level measures. Thus, narcissism's weaker association with dispositional aggression may reflect the failure of such assessments to account for situational triggers.

At the unconditional level, the raw observed sex differences across BPAQ dimensions broadly align with previous findings: men score substantially higher in physical aggression, slightly higher in verbal aggression, and do not consistently differ from women in hostility (A. H. Buss & Perry, 1992; Jain et al., 2023). Anger is one exception to this correspondence: although higher scores among women have also been reported (Romero et al., 2024), this pattern is not consistently established in the literature (A. H. Buss & Perry, 1992; Webster et al., 2014). Moreover, our data suggest that raw differences in verbal aggression may be driven by measurement non-invariance. The remaining difference in physical aggression is consistent with sexual-selection accounts emphasizing greater male engagement in direct intrasexual competition (Puts et al., 2015).

The general shift of the expected scores in favor of women after conditioning on the Dark Triad suggests that unconditional differences partly overlap with sex differences in aversive traits. However, the moderation results qualify an interpretation of the male-Dark Triad overlap as evidence that aversive traits specifically channel male contest competition into aggressive dispositions. If interpreted through contest competition, this pattern implies a mechanism that may also operate among women, with male predominance driven mainly by differences in the distribution of Dark Triad scores between sexes. Conditional differences in hostility, verbal aggression and anger also raise questions about the interpretation of men as more dispositionally aggressive. Men's higher Dark Triad scores should, by themselves, predict greater scores across these subscales. Yet women generally report equivalent levels of hostility (A. H. Buss & Perry, 1992; Jain et al., 2023) and, in this case, equivalent levels of verbal aggression and higher levels of anger. If cognitive-and possibly affective-aggressive dispositions can be interpreted as reflecting a tendency toward indirect forms of intrasexual competition, then we are led to a symmetric interpretation: aversive traits similarly enhance direct and indirect forms of intrasexual competition. Women's higher baseline levels of the latter then suggest a complementary mechanism that offsets their lower average levels of Dark Triad traits, although this remains an open research question.

Our original account located sex differentiation in the expression of aversive traits, where sexual selection was expected to strengthen the translation of these traits into direct aggression among men and into hostility among women. The results instead suggest this differentiation may be upstream. A revised interpretation under the framework of intrasexual competition may be that selection operates at the frequency (Wilson, 1994) at which these traits emerge within sexes, rather than on how they implement competitive strategies. We note that this interpretation remains tentative, as the current design cannot rule out competing explanations for the observed pattern.

Considerable debate in the Dark Triad literature concerns how best to study the associations of these strongly overlapping traits with external outcomes (Furnham et al., 2014; Sleep et al., 2017). One widely adopted approach invokes a common Dark Core underlying this overlap (D. N. Jones & Figueredo, 2013; Vize et al., 2020) and uses bifactor models to distinguish associations attributable to the general component from those unique to each trait. However, bifactor models leave the structure against which residual coefficients are interpreted implicit. The oblique VWLE expresses a trait's first-order association while holding only specific sibling components and non-sibling variables fixed. It therefore extends the first-order interpretation directly available for the reference facet in an S -1 model to non-reference traitsfoot_4 . For psychopathy, this means relaxing conditioning on the Machiavellianism reference while retaining adjustment for the narcissism-specific component. In the present study, this translation shows how the reference facet and trait-specific associations combine: they reinforce one another for psychopathy but largely cancel out for narcissism. The translations are nontrivial in magnitude. For hostility, a substantial unique effect of psychopathy produces a barely noticeable difference between psychopathy and the reference Machiavellianism at the first-order level. By contrast, the unique associations involving psychopathy markedly differentiate first-order psychopathy from Machiavellianism in the other equations. Thus, VWLE may bridge the gap between theory and estimation by making the substantive implications of residual coefficients explicit.

Several limitations qualify these results. Most importantly, the BPAQ does not provide a dedicated measure of indirect aggression, and our conclusions rely on hostility as an empirically motivated approximation (Archer & Webb, 2006). Both the operationalization of predictions and the interpretations concerning intrasexual competition should therefore be regarded as suggestive. Future studies should employ dedicated measures of both direct and indirect aggression, and also distinguish aggression toward same-sex versus other-sex targets explicitly. Second, the SD3 provides relatively narrow measurements of multidimensional traits, while the modest fit and reliability of some of its factors further limit construct coverage and precision-a finding that resonates with the wider literature regarding the scale's psychometric properties (Knitter et al., 2025). More comprehensive assessments of the Dark Triad traits are therefore needed. Relatedly, meaningful absolute estimates and asymptotic inference do not allow us to conclusively rule out sex differences opposite to the predicted direction for physical and verbal aggression on psychopathy (see Table B2). Better measurements may help clarify this question. Finally, because the findings rely on cross-sectional self-reports of dispositions, their extension to competitive and aggressive behavior in real-world settings remains to be examined.

VWLE should likewise be regarded as a descriptive pilot implementation. Although the estimator is supported by a mathematical proof and preliminary empirical validation (see Table E1), its broader statistical properties remain to be established. The bootstrap standard errors give a provisional indication of sampling variability, but analytic standard errors have not yet been derived. Exactness of the first-order reconstruction under the current feasible least-squares implementation assumes orthogonality between direct-general and specific factor loadings (see Section E.3).

5. Conclusion

Our findings reproduce a broad pattern of associations consistently reported in the Dark Triad and aggression literature and suggest that it may hold for both women and men. By introducing the VWLE, we provide the first substantive translation of this component-level pattern into associations involving the original traits. The present study therefore contributes to the consolidation of the field's main empirical findings within a common substantive framework. The bifactor model answers how shared and specific components from a set of overlapping factors relate to an outcome. VWLE then answers what those component-level associations imply for the factors themselves.

A.2. Reliability

Table A3 presents Cronbach's alpha and McDonald's omega reliability estimates for the BPAQ and SD3 scale scores. BPAQ reliability is consistent with previous findings (Andreu Rodríguez et al., 2002; Valdivia-Peralta et al., 2014), with Cronbach's alphas of 0.79 for physical aggression, 0.69 for verbal aggression, 0.75 for hostility, and 0.77 for anger. SD3 estimates are likewise consistent with previous findings for Machiavellianism (α = 0.74) and narcissism (α = 0.62) (D. N. Jones & Paulhus, 2014; Pineda et al., 2020). Psychopathy reliability is somewhat lower than previously reported (α = 0.63), with two items exhibiting negligible standardized factor loadings ( λstd = 0.07 and λstd = -0.00).

A.3. Invariance

Table A4 reports changes in model fit across varying measurement invariance model restrictions. Robust CFI values are calculated using a common independence model following Little et al. (2007). Changes in fit for both partial scalar specifications are calculated relative to the metric model. Commonly used guidelines reviewed by Putnick and Bornstein (2016) consider decreases in CFI of .010 alongside increases in RMSEA of .015 or SRMR of .030 for metric and .015 for scalar invariance as indications of noninvariance, although these thresholds are not universal.

Table A4. Invariance fit metrics BPAQ CFI ∆CFI RMSEA ∆RMSEA SRMR ∆SRMR Configural .8485 -.0598 -.0663 -Metric .8366 -.0119 .0611 .0013 .0755 .0092 Scalar .7982 -.0384 .0668 .0057 .0816 .0061 Partial .8317 -.0048 .0613 .0002 .0765 .0010 SD3 Configural .8327 -.0541 -.0589 -Metric .8343 .0017 .0521 -.0020 .0634 .0046 Scalar .8062 -.0281 .0553 .0032 .0672 .0037 Partial .8238 -.0105 .0529 .0008 .0653 .0018 Note. Blockwise multigroup Aggression (BPAQ) and Dark Triad (SD3) measurement model fit metrics across women and men. Dark Triad measurement uses a bifactor (S -1) with Machiavellianism as the reference facet.

The configural model specifies the same factor structure with loadings and item intercepts freely estimated across groups; the metric model constrains factor loadings to equality across groups; the scalar model additionally constrains item intercepts; the partial model frees constraints on the item intercepts whose differences between groups show the largest contributions to the likelihood function under regularization. BPAQ = Buss and Perry Aggression Questionnaire; SD3 = Short Dark Triad; CFI = robust comparative fit index; RMSEA = robust root mean square error of approximation; SRMR = standardized root mean square residual. Robust CFI values were calculated using a common independence model with item means and variances constrained equal across groups. ∆ denotes the current model's value minus the preceding model's value. Changes in the partial model are expressed with respect to the metric model. Models were estimated using robust maximum likelihood.

Constraining factor loadings to equality across women and men produces negligible changes in fit in the SD3 and small changes in the BPAQ, broadly supporting metric invariance. Additional equality constraints on item intercepts yield mixed evidence for scalar invariance: robust CFI decreases by .038 for the BPAQ and .028 for the SD3, whereas RMSEA and SRMR increase only slightly (.006 for both indices in the BPAQ and .003 and .004 for the SD3, respectively). A partial scalar invariance specification further frees item intercepts whose difference between groups show the largest contributions to the likelihood function. To identify non-invariant item intercepts, we use lasso regularized CFA with 10-fold cross-validation to rank candidate intercept differences. Following this ranking, we fit successive partial scalar-invariant models, freeing one additional item intercept at each step. In each model, we test the between-group differences in all freed intercepts. We retain the specification immediately preceding the first model in which any freed intercept difference has an absolute z statistic below 1.96, the critical value for a two-tailed test at α = .05. All remaining item intercepts remain constrained to equality across groups. For the BPAQ, following this procedure frees 7 out of the 29 items (3 out of 9 for physical aggression, 1 out of 5 for verbal aggression, 2 out of 8 for hostility, and 1 out of 7 for anger). For the SD3, the procedure frees 4 out of the 27 items (3 out of 9 for narcissism and 1 out of 9 for psychopathy). Across scales, the partial specifications are in line with conventional guidelines.

A.4. Linearity

To assess whether the linear treatment of ordinal item responses may contribute to modest configural fit, we re-estimate the configural measurement models using diagonally weighted least squares (DWLS), with robust standard errors and a mean-and variance-adjusted test statistic. All items are treated as ordered categorical variables. Robust CFI values are calculated using a common independence baseline with item thresholds constrained equal across groups. Neither ordinal specification improves fit over its linear counterpart, giving worse absolute metrics across fit indices (BPAQ: CFI = .713, RMSEA = .095, SRMR = .078; SD3: CFI = .662, RMSEA = .084, SRMR = .074).

A.5. Residual covariances

To address concerns over modest measurement fit (Hu & Bentler, 1999) influencing structural analyses, we construct an alternative measurement specification relaxing some residual covariance constraints. Using lasso regularization, we identify and freely estimate the residual covariances with the largest contributions to model likelihood: 12 of 406 possible covariances for the BPAQ and 10 of 351 for the SD3. Table A5 presents the resulting fit indices. Configural CFI values exceed .90 for both questionnaires (BPAQ: .915; SD3: .903), alongside low RMSEA (.046 and .042) and SRMR (.060 and .054). Full scalar constraints continue to produce appreciable deterioration in CFI, whereas partial scalar specifications show limited additional misfit relative to the metric models. We use this alternative specification to replicate our main results in Table B6.

A.6. Higher-order representation

Table A6 presents standardized loadings and communalities from a second-order measurement model for the Dark Triad. Machiavellianism shows the strongest standardized loading (λ = .964) on the general Dark Core factor, followed by psychopathy (λ = .886) and narcissism (λ = .473). Thus, the general factor accounts for almost all (93%) of the latent variance in Machiavellianism, compared with 78.5% in psychopathy and 22.4% in narcissism.

A.7. Bifactor latent covariances

Table A7 presents standardized residual covariances between the non-reference facets under alternative bifactor (S -1) specifications. These correspond to latent partial cor-relations controlling for the respective reference facet. Smaller absolute values indicate less shared variance remaining between the non-reference facets, providing a basis for assessing which reference facet most comprehensively captures the variance shared across the Dark Triad.

Using Machiavellianism as the reference facet leaves a negligible standardized residual association between the psychopathy and narcissism specific factors ( φstd = 0.062). In contrast, using psychopathy or narcissism as the reference facet leaves moderate to large residual associations between the remaining specific factors. Taken together with the second-order model, in which the general factor accounted for almost all of the latent variance in Machiavellianism, this pattern supports Machiavellianism as the reference facet that most closely represents the variance shared across the SD3 traits in our sample.
