The primary Machiavellianism reference columns broadly align with both the diagonal pattern of associations implied by the alternating reference facets (in bold) and the psychopathy reference columns: psychopathy and Machiavellianism show the strongest associations with aggression, with psychopathy generally predominating, while narcissism shows comparatively small associations. The latter representations nevertheless assign slightly more weight to the predictive effect of narcissism at the first-order level across outcomes.

On the other hand, the correlated three-factor model illustrates a known pattern: conditioning on overlapping traits can obscure associations carried by their shared variance (Furnham et al., 2014). In this case, over-conditioningfoot_5 would have us infer approximately double the magnitude for the effect of psychopathy across verbal aggression and anger while compensating with a sign flip for Machiavellianism (see Table D3 for anger estimates). There is also a noticeable degree of correspondence between the correlated three-factor model and the bifactor under the narcissism reference, which poorly accounts for the shared variance among the Dark Triad (see Sections A.6 and A.7). This correspondence is most visible in the aforementioned larger psychopathy estimates for verbal aggression and anger and the smaller Machiavellianism estimates across outcomes.

Estimation stability also differs between specifications. Across bootstrap iterations, the Machiavellianism and psychopathy references produce the highest rates of admissible solutionsfoot_6 , with converging measurement stages and positive definite covariance structures at 92.8% and 88.5%, respectively. The correlated three-factor and narcissismreference models produce the lowest rates, at 50.8% and 38.5%, respectively. The covariance structure of the narcissism-reference model is already fragile at the full sample, and estimation becomes feasible only by removing the age covariate from the imputation model.

B.2. Bootstrap

The full-pipeline bootstrap repeats measurement fitting, composed imputation model fitting, plausible-value generation, structural estimation, and VWLE reconstruction. Regularization is not repeated, as this is computationally infeasible; the selected partialinvariance constraints remain fixed. To be considered admissible, measurement and imputation fits must converge, yield non-Heywood estimates and also yield a positivedefinite factor-score uncertainty covariance matrix, evaluated through a Cholesky decomposition. Unsuccessful structural fits are omitted from plausible-value pooling, and failed bootstrap attempts are replaced until 9,999 successful resamples are obtained. Factor signs are aligned with the full-sample solution using loading-column cosines across all indicators loading on each factor. Corrections extend to interactions and VWLEs. Low absolute cosines do not constitute an exclusion criterion.

Table B2 examines disagreement between full-sample and bootstrap inference for the main and interaction effects of sex in physical and verbal aggression in the model with all Dark Triad-by-sex interactions (see Table D2). Bootstrap means remain close to the full-sample estimates, but bootstrap standard errors are consistently larger. This increase is most pronounced in the contested Psychopathy-by-sex interactions, whose bootstrap standard errors are more than twice their full-sample counterparts. The main effect of sex on verbal aggression remains significant under both procedures. Finite-PV Monte Carlo noise accounts for less than 1% of bootstrap variance across the reported coefficients. All 25 plausible-value structural fits were successful in every accepted bootstrap resample.

Tables B3 and B4 examine potential bias associated with the high proportion of discarded resamples in the narcissism-reference and correlated three-factor models. Bootstrap means remain generally close to the full-sample estimates, with maximum absolute differences of .064 and .043, respectively. Bootstrap standard errors are consistently larger than their full-sample counterparts, indicating that increased uncertainty remains the principal difference between the procedures. Finite-PV Monte Carlo noise accounts for less than 1% of bootstrap variance across both models. All 25 plausible-value structural fits were successful in every accepted bootstrap resample. These comparisons show limited displacement in the centers of the accepted bootstrap distributions, although they cannot exclude selection effects associated with discarding inadmissible resamples.

B.4. Fit sensitivity

Table B6 compares structural estimates with residual item covariances fixed at zero versus selected covariances freely estimated (see Table A5). The overall pattern remains similar: the reference facet and psychopathy retain positive associations with all aggression outcomes, while the negative psychopathy-by-sex interactions for physical and verbal aggression persist. Thus, improving measurement model fit produces limited changes in the substantive results.

E.1.2. First-order structural model

Let denote the linear structural model of endogenous η on exogenous first-order ξ (1) , where we consider the simpler case with no endogenous predictors for notation clarity.

This model has also been called an extended first-order factor model (Eid et al., 2018). We are interested in the vector of coefficients γ ⊤ . However, if ξ (1) has a nested or overlapping factor structure, the direct first-order estimands will not correspond, in general, to the target first-order effects. By the Frisch-Waugh-Lovell theorem (FWL -Frisch & Waugh, 1933; Lovell, 1963), conditioning on sibling variables distributes the effect of the general component across the overlapping block, making the effects for the ξ (1) j ∈ ξ (1) defined with respect to a residual coordinate composed of their specific component plus the part of the general factor not linearly recovered by the remaining sibling factors.

See section E.8 for a formal derivation.

E.1.3. Reduced form structural model

One solution to this problem is to substitute the first-order model with a reduced form, where each general factor (i.e., the source of overlap) appears only once on the right hand side, as opposed to being nested across multiple first-order variables:

Now, allowing heterogeneous effects gives what has been called an extended bifactor model with criterion variables (Eid et al., 2018), where γ ⊤ g contains the effects for the general factors and γ ⊤ s the effects for the residual or specific components of each first-order variable:

Estimating this model solves the problem of overlap by isolating the effect of the general factor instead of having it distributed across sibling variables. However, raw coefficient estimates still do not, in general, map back to the substantive constructs of interest.

The variance geometry of weights determines the target best linear predictor parametrization reconstructed by the VWLE. For example, the first-order VWLE with Φ (1) uses the full variance information and expresses the conditional effect holding all the other first-order predictors fixed. E.3. Feasible estimation

The form of the VWLE estimand highlights a tension in the feasibility of the estimation procedure. On the one hand, fitting the reduced-form model requires a bifactor measurement for the specification of the reduced-form predictors in the structural model. On the other hand, the bifactor measurement model does not directly provide the higher-order loading matrix Λ ξ , which is required for the VWLE weights. Under proportionality (Yung et al., 1999) implied by a Schmid-Leiman (Schmid & Leiman, 1957) factorization, the bifactor model gives the lower-order loading matrix Λ x and the composite matrix

The Schmid and Leiman (1957) solution to the set of higher-order loading matrices requires recursive partition on the latent block until either the variance-covariance of the highest-order factors is identity or a single highest-order factor is found. It also requires the unique factor disturbances at each level of recursion be orthogonal. This last requirement can be restrictive in practice, as a number of variables may not want to be decomposed to orthogonality. The oblique bifactor model implemented in this article is a direct illustration, as it allows residual associations between specific factor components. Nonetheless, the identity in Equation (E12) can be used to recover the higher-order loading matrix from the parameters estimated within the bifactor framework. Following Rosseel and Loh (2024), let M denote a mapping matrix satisfying MΛ x = I. Since Λ x is not square in general, we use a left inverse, which exists provided that Λ x has full column rank. Any such left inverse satisfies this property. Premultiplying the composite loading matrix gives an exact recovery of the corresponding higher-order loading matrix. This recovery is directly feasible from the bifactor solution when its general-loading matrix coincides with Λ xξ.

Yung et al. (1999) study the proportionality constraint property of the Schmid-Leiman factorization and regard it a special case within the general hierarchical model family. They establish the translation between the unconstrained general hierarchical factor model and the higher-order model with (constrained) direct effects of the general factor on manifest indicators. For the two-layer-i.e., bifactor-model, this becomes where Λ D is a matrix of direct loadings of the manifest indicators on the general factors ξ g .

Expansion of the first-order block illustrates the redundancy problem in the general higher-order factor model identified by Yung et al. (1999), where direct effects Λ D are not separately identifiable from indirect effects Λ x Λ ξ without imposing constraints.

The general hierarchical factor model instead avoids this redundant parameterization by estimating the combined direct and indirect loading matrix:

Equation (E15) characterizes the limitation of Equation (E13) in recovering Λ ξ . Under non-proportionality, the general bifactor model gives the matrix Λ xg , and left-inverse multiplication gives shrink relative to the corresponding specific loadings. Finally, let M (LS) denote the Moore-Penrose left inverse of Λ x . Choosing this convention leads to the least-squares solution

This convention absorbs the component of direct loadings aligned with the column space of Λ x into the reconstructed higher-order loadings. It yields exact recovery when the direct and specific loading vectors are orthogonal within each cluster, such that Λ ⊤ x Λ D = 0. For any given convention, the residual direct-loading matrix associated with the reconstruction is

These residuals satisfy the selected convention by construction: anchor residuals are zero, cluster residual sums are zero, or residuals are orthogonal to the specific-loading columns. The conditions stated for exact recovery instead concern the population direct loadings Λ D . Importantly, these three conventions give locally differentiable reconstructions and therefore permit subsequent delta-method derivation of standard errors using the appropriate joint sampling covariance under regular estimation conditions.

E.5. Corollary: pooled standardization

Under the stratified two-stage PV framework, components are standardized using their pooled full sample moments within each imputation. This changes their units and requires a corresponding transformation of the VWLE estimates. Let D g and D s be diagonal matrices containing the pooled standard deviations of the general and specific components, respectively, and let µ g and µ s denote their corresponding pooled mean vectors. E.6. Equivalent auxiliary representation

The oblique (type-2) VWLE implemented in this article targets the partial effect of a first-order factor while holding all non-overlapping components and covariates fixed. Table E1 illustrates this interpretation by comparing VWLEs computed from the saturated exploratory model specification with the corresponding direct parametrizations of the oblique first-order effects. Preregistration

The preregistration is available at https://osf.io/w9xup/overview.

Two changes to the preregistered model specifications warrant clarification. First, we included sex as a predictor of all four aggression outcomes in the C1 and subsequent structural models. The preregistered C1 equations omitted sex for hostility and anger because differences were not predicted for these outcomes. However, estimating these equations with and without sex revealed misspecification that propagated through the system, affecting focal predictors in neighboring equations. Second, the data did not satisfy the assumptions required for an identified symmetric bifactor model (Eid et al., 2017). We therefore adopted a bifactor S-1 specification.

Replication package

Data, analysis code, and saved bootstrap results are available at https://github.com/nicolasgonzalezr/dark-triad-aggression-replication.

Appendix E. Variance-Weighted Latent Effect

The variance-weighted latent effect (VWLE) is the model-implied estimand that reconstructs first-order effects from a bifactor model by weighting general and specific component effects according to the variance structure implied by the measurement model. The oblique or type-two VWLE implemented in this article is the reduced-form best linear predictor that relaxes conditioning on a latent block's overlapping general factor.

E.1.1. Orthogonal decomposition of first-order latent predictors

Assume the vector of first-order latent predictors ξ (1) , admits a first-order linear decomposition given by ξ (1) = Λ ξ ξ g + ξ s , where ξ g is a vector of general latent factors Λ ξ a matrix of loadings of the first-order variables on the general factors and ξ s is a vector of residual or specific components (Schmid & Leiman, 1957). General and specific components within each overlapping block are orthogonal, but specific components may be correlated. The measurement model can be represented most clearly in proportional 7 (Yung et al., 1999) oblique bifactor form:

The first-order loading matrix is assumed to have a simple structure, and any zero row in Λ ξ collapses the bifactor structure to accommodate non-nested factors. Control covariates are also represented inside the ξ s vector, with unity loading for manifest variables. The implied covariance is: where

Yung et al. (1999) further discuss the conditions and alternative sets of identifying constraints that yield unique solutions for Λ x Λ ξ and Λ D from a model given by Equation (E15). Among these constraints, they propose selecting cluster item anchors by setting their direct general loading to zero; and also a so-called residual direct effects method, where the sum of direct effects for each cluster is set to zero. Importing these identifying conventions into the mapping matrix approach lets us characterize the recovery assumptions implied by Equation (E16). First, let A denote an anchor selection matrix with the same dimensions as Λ x , constructed by setting one entry per cluster column to unity at the selected anchor item, with all other entries set to zero. Each anchor must have a non-zero loading on its corresponding specific factor. Choosing the anchor constraint convention leads to

The recovery error is therefore determined by the direct loadings at the selected anchor items relative to their corresponding specific loadings in Λ x . Anchors are chosen among items thought to have no direct paths from ξ g -yielding exact recovery when this holds and approaching exact recovery as the anchors' direct-to-specific loading ratios approach zero. Alternatively, let R denote a cluster membership matrix corresponding to the residual direct effects method (Yung et al., 1999). Let this matrix have the same dimensions as Λ x , with unity when an item belongs to the corresponding cluster and zero otherwise. Membership is determined by the specified measurement structure. Choosing the zero-sum constraint then leads to

This inverse requires a non-zero sum of specific loadings within each cluster. The recovery error is given by the cluster sums of direct loadings divided by the corresponding sums of specific loadings, yielding exact recovery when direct loadings have mean zero within each cluster, and approaching exact recovery as the direct loadings regressors using the feasible least-squares reconstruction on regression factor scores. Then, for each target facet in the original saturated specification, we fit an auxiliary model jointly replacing the S -1 reference regressor, the target specific component, and their component-by-sex terms with the reconstructed first-order regressor and its interaction with sex. The results confirm the expected behavior of the oblique VWLE estimator, yielding numerically equivalent point estimates for both main and interaction effects from a single reference-model fit and multiple auxiliary fits using direct parametrizations of the corresponding oblique first-order effects.

E.7. Equivalent multigroup representation

Under the current stratified two-stage framework (von Hippel, 2009), VWLE estimates combine information from the multigroup measurement model and the pooled structural model, assuming compatibility of the stratified factor loadings and bifactor orthogonality restrictions with the pooled structural covariance. However, metric invariance supports common factor loadings, and within-sex bifactor orthogonality carries over to the sex-adjusted pooled covariance by the law of total covariance. Table E2 corroborates point estimate equivalence between unstandardized VWLEs obtained from the primary pooled-interaction structural parametrization and an alternative multigroup structural parametrization. As the focus of this exercise is on point estimate equivalence, we present estimates obtained from a simpler factor-score regression framework.
